source: University of California Statewide IPM Program (UC ANR) - Garlic Disease Guidelines
title: Garlic Leaf Blight and Botrytis Leaf Blight Complex (Botrytis porri / Stemphylium vesicarium / Alternaria porri)
content: Garlic leaf blight is the most important garlic (Allium sativum L.) foliar disease worldwide in cool temperate and Mediterranean climates and is caused by a complex of three necrotrophic filamentous fungi: Botrytis porri (teleomorph Botryotinia porri; causes Botrytis leaf blight, the most prevalent in the United States and northern Europe), Stemphylium vesicarium (syn. S. allii; causes Stemphylium leaf blight, SLB, the most destructive in southern Europe, Mexico, Chile, Argentina, California, and the Pacific Northwest), and Alternaria porri (causes purple blotch, secondary in most areas but the primary agent in parts of Africa, India, and Southeast Asia). Because all three fungi produce morphologically similar necrotic blight lesions on garlic foliage, and because they routinely occur together in mixed infections on the same leaf, the whole complex is often referred to collectively as 'garlic leaf blight' by growers in many regions. Severe epidemics reduce plant photosynthetic leaf area by 30-80%, reduce bulb size and marketable weight by 25-60%, and promote secondary bacterial bulb rots in storage. Symptoms first appear on the oldest (outermost) leaves 3-6 weeks after emergence as small, elongated, water-soaked or pale gray 2-5 mm lesions near the leaf tip. Botrytis porri lesions expand rapidly during cool, wet (12-18 C) weather into large, boat-shaped, sunken, tan-to-gray-white lesions 2-4 cm long with a distinct dark brown to purplish-brown margin; under humid conditions a dense gray to brown felt-like layer of Botrytis conidiophores and chains of one-celled conidia develops in lesion centers. Stemphylium vesicarium lesions are smaller (5-15 mm), distinctly oval to elongated, sunken, tan with small purple-brown borders, and they develop small, raised, black, clavate pseudothecial-like perithecia with long beaks in concentric rings within the lesion center after about 10 days; the perithecia are the ascigerous form (Pleospora allii or Pleospora tarda) and are highly diagnostic for Stemphylium. Alternaria porri (purple blotch) lesions are larger (1-2 x 2-5 cm), target-shaped with concentric zonate rings of dark brown to purple-black conidia-bearing conidiophores. With all three agents, multiple lesions coalesce to blight entire leaves 2-4 weeks after initial infection; entire garlic scapes (flowering stalks) can be blighted, reducing bulbil and seed production. Severe blight causes premature dieback of the entire garlic plant 2-4 weeks before normal maturity, severely curtailing bulb bulbing. All three pathogens survive in a semi-saprophytic state on infected Allium crop debris (garlic, onion, leek, shallot, wild Allium weeds); they also survive as sclerotia (B. porri produces 2-5 mm black sclerotia on dead leaf tissue and bulb neck scales) and as pseudothecia (Stemphylium, Alternaria sexual fruiting) for 1-3 years on the soil surface. They are also carried internally and externally on garlic seed garlic cloves and on infested planting stock: this is the main mechanism of long-distance spread within and between countries. Conidia of all three organisms are splash-dispersed by rain and overhead irrigation over 1-5 m distances; longer distance spread occurs via wind-dispersed conidia in turbulent boundary layer flow. Infection requires 4-16 hours of leaf wetness at temperatures of 10-25 C; latent period is 5-10 days depending on temperature. Management: (1) plant only inspected, blight-free seed garlic cloves produced in arid seed-increase regions (e.g. the traditional garlic seed-increase areas of Gilroy CA, southern Idaho, and Mendoza, Argentina); hot-water seed garlic treatment at 49 C for 20 minutes combined with thiram + carboxin fungicide dusting before planting reduces clove-borne inoculum by >95%. (2) long 3-4 year crop rotations away from Allium species (garlic, onion, shallot, leek, chives, green onion, bunching onion) and prompt fall tillage to bury Allium crop debris. (3) wild Allium weed management especially wild garlic (Allium vineale), wild onion (A. canadense), field garlic (A. oleraceum), and three-cornered leek (A. triquetrum) in field borders, irrigation ditches, and fence rows because they are reservoirs for the entire leaf blight complex. (4) cultural practices: drip irrigation instead of overhead sprinklers; wide plant spacing (8-15 cm between cloves in 30 cm rows), north-south oriented rows to improve air movement and leaf drying; plant at the correct planting depth (2-3 x clove width) and avoid excessive nitrogen which promotes lush foliage and increases susceptibility to Botrytis. (5) genetic resistance: several garlic selections (A. sativum var. ophioscorodon cultivars 'German White', 'Georgian Fire', 'Spanish Roja', 'Italian Late', and a few A. longicuspis accessions) show partial quantitative resistance to the Stemphylium-Botrytis complex and are the basis of current Allium breeding programs; no commercial cultivar is fully immune. (6) fungicide programs in conventional production: begin protectant sprays at the first sign of leaf lesions in early spring and continue on 7-14 day intervals until 3 weeks before harvest. Best performing materials in Cornell and UC IPM trials: FRAC 2 dicarboximides (iprodione, vinclozolin) are highly effective against Botrytis, FRAC 3 DMI (tebuconazole, difenoconazole, prothioconazole, metconazole, fluquinconazole) excellent on Stemphylium and Alternaria, FRAC 7 SDHI (fluxapyroxad, boscalid, pyraziflumid, isofetamid) + FRAC 11 QoI (azoxystrobin, pyraclostrobin, picoxystrobin) premixes provide broad-spectrum control of all three fungi but must be alternated with non-SDHI/QoI materials and tank-mixed with multi-site FRAC M3/M1 partners (mancozeb, copper) because B. porri and S. vesicarium develop resistance rapidly to single-SOI chemistries. Organic programs are based on copper + sulphur, potassium bicarbonate, Reynoutria sachalinensis extract, and Bacillus subtilis/amyloliquefaciens QST 713/MBI 600 rotations but rarely provide more than 40-60% protection during high-blight-pressure cool wet springs.
